item.description:
Why this matters: Advanced threat activity — review privileged access, persistence detection, and lateral-movement controls.

The PHP2Shell saga continues, with attackers discovering new ways to exploit the critical vulnerability impacting millions of organizations worldwide.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has warned of a high severity Linux kernel privilege escalation flaw that attackers are chaining with PHP2Shell bugs in the wild.

Identified as CVE-2026-46300, it could allow attackers to run malicious code with root permissions, giving them unrestricted ability to run commands, tamper with system settings, view, edit, or delete files, and perform other malicious actions.

Once attackers establish root access, they can perform any action on a server including, but not limited to, disabling the server, creating accounts, removing accounts, connecting to other servers, and adding/removing software, explained Scott Miserendino, CTO at security and compliance platform DataBee.

This approach allowed Volt Typhoon to carry out exploitation and post-exploitation activity securely while reducing the risk of detection, attribution, and disruption.”

item.title: 🔴 New Cisco firewall zero-day being actively exploited
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

A high-severity flaw in the Remote Access SSL VPN service of Cisco Secure Firewall Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) and Cisco Secure Firewall Threat Defense (FTD) is under active exploitation to crash vulnerable devices.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-76418 and rated 8.6 in severity, is due to logic errors when secondary authentication is configured on a tunnel group, Cisco said in its advisory. It could allow a remote, unauthenticated attacker to send a crafted request when connecting to the SSL remote access VPN that results in a device reload and thus denial of service.

Vulnerable products

item.description:

New research from cybersecurity company Cofense describes a phishing campaign that hooks overeager enterprise users by making them think they are getting an invite to a private invite-only Anthropic preview.

In reality, adversarial actors are trying to steal Google and Microsoft login credentials, exploiting video teleconferencing software GoTo Webinar branding to do so.

“It sells exclusivity,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. “Fear of missing out is the oldest lure in the book.”

item.title: 🟠 Anthropic and OpenAI diverge on who should pull the plug on risky AI
item.description:
Why this matters: Advanced threat activity — review privileged access, persistence detection, and lateral-movement controls.

OpenAI and Anthropic agree that frontier AI systems need stronger oversight, but they are proposing sharply different approaches to stopping models that pose serious risks: Anthropic wants courts empowered to suspend dangerous systems, while OpenAI argues developers should be required to maintain and use effective shutdown controls.

The proposals appear in separate submissions to California Governor Gavin Newsom following his September 18 executive order directing state officials to consider additional safeguards for frontier AI systems. Both companies support independent safety assessments and expanded reporting of incidents involving AI systems that act beyond their intended permissions.

“If the AG concludes, informed by the independent evaluation, that a frontier AI company’s models pose a near-term risk of catastrophic harm, they should be able to seek a court order to suspend a model’s deployment, internal use, or further development,” Anthropic wrote…

item.title: 🔵 Imposter abused trust in OpenAI, Anthropic, and 30 others to hunt for secrets
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Attackers are impersonating AI agents from companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta in a bid to trick organizations into exposing sensitive credentials, according to researchers who observed a single threat actor cycling through dozens of fake bot identities while probing enterprise web servers for secrets.

A single threat actor was seen posing as approximately 32 AI bots, while probing organizations across multiple industries. Sought files included those used to store passwords, API keys, and cloud credentials.

A malicious scanner used by the attacker ran from an unnamed major cloud provider. “It ignores web pages and requests files that commonly store secrets, including .env configuration files, cloud credential files, private SSH keys, and server environment data, working from a list of roughly 90 file paths,” Cequence’s director of threat research, Will Glazier, said in a blog post.

The finding represents more of a comeback than a fresh surge because in Q1 LevelBlue already recorded vulnerabilities as the root cause in 20% of the intrusions it investigated.

In both Q1 and the latest figures known security vulnerabilities in edge devices made them the prime target for exploitation.

item.title: 🟠 Securing MCP servers before the AI rollout outpaces security
item.description:
Why this matters: Potential data exposure — review monitoring and incident-response readiness.

Your company’s CTO has a plan to implement your company’s first LLM-based application. The board approved it, and now you’re finding out about it. It’s a typical story I hear all the time, and I’ve lived it myself.

You’ve heard everything about models and LLMs, but now you see this new term all over the place: Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers —and the realization that you now need to make sure they are implemented securely.

What is an MCP server?

MCP servers are like the ODBC of the 1990s. Before ODBC, every application needed custom code to query databases. ODBC defined a single standard on how to talk to databases, and database vendors just developed a driver to talk to their solution.

item.title: 🔴 PHP2Shell will persist in enterprise environments for years
item.description:
Why this matters: Supply-chain risk — review third-party access and affected vendor dependencies.

Two critical vulnerabilities were announced last week in PHP, the internet’s most widely used web application runtime, and they came with the familiar warning to patch immediately. But CISOs will have to deal with the long tail of these flaws for years due to widespread PHP integration into third-party products with patching cycles customers don’t control.

NAS devices, firewalls, VPN gateways, printers, building management panels, industrial IoT devices, and human-machine interfaces (HMIs) inside operational technology (OT) networks have web panels powered by PHP runtimes that cannot be patched directly. And many of these runtimes have unsupported versions for which upstream patches are not available.

item.title: 🟠 Gheist turns GitHub Actions into a secret extraction service
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

A threat actor dubbed Gheist is turning compromised GitHub accounts into credential-harvesting platforms. By planting malicious GitHub Actions workflows in private repositories, the attackers can expose repository and environment secrets, then retrieve them through GitHub APIs before deleting evidence of the activity.

Tracked since September 15 by Wiz Research, the campaign has left more than 13,500 malicious branches across over 850 compromised accounts, spanning personal projects and private enterprise repositories.

The campaign’s weapon is GitHub Actions, the platform’s automation service, which attackers are using to turn stolen access into harvested credentials. The automation creates a branch, adds a workflow named “sync-check” that attempts to print secrets into execution logs, retrieves those logs through the GitHub API, and deletes the workflow run seconds later.

item.title: 🔴 When prevention fails: Why cyber resilience is the next big test of trust
item.description:
Why this matters: Elevated ransomware risk — validate backups, endpoint protection, and recovery readiness.

Imagine arriving at work on a Monday morning to find employees cannot log in, customer service is unavailable, and critical business applications have stopped working. Security alerts are flashing. The IT team is investigating. Business leaders want to know when operations will resume.

Then comes the question everyone hopes they never have to ask: Can we recover safely, and how long will it take?

Most organizations have invested in cybersecurity, from firewalls to identity controls to monitoring tools and backup systems. Yet a serious cyberattack can still disrupt operations, damage customer trust, and leave teams unsure which systems and data they can rely on.

This is driving a shift in cybersecurity, moving beyond preventing attacks toward building organizations that can withstand disruption, recover safely and learn from incidents. That is the essence of cyber resilience.

item.title: 🔴 10 ways attackers abuse AI services to hack your business
item.description:
Why this matters: Elevated ransomware risk — validate backups, endpoint protection, and recovery readiness.

Attackers are starting to exploit AI systems to mount attacks in the same way they once relied on built-in enterprise tools such as PowerShell.

Instead of relying on malware, cybercriminals are increasingly abusing AI tools enterprises depend on — a trend some experts describe as “living off the AI land.” The expanded abuse of AI ecosystems features a growing array of tactics, including poisoned models, compromised MCP servers, prompt injection attacks, and AI supply-chain vulnerabilities.

“We’re seeing it in things like poisoned MCP servers in the supply chain, attackers using legitimate models like Claude to extract sensitive data, and even viral agents like OpenClaw accidentally causing destructive actions,” says Kaushik Shanadi, CTO at Helmet Security, a startup focused on securing agentic AI communications. “The problem is most of these systems were deployed before anyone stopped to think about governance or security.”

item.title: 🟠 Attackers compromised 42 GitHub repositories by using files too large to be searched
item.description:
Why this matters: Supply-chain risk — review third-party access and affected vendor dependencies.

A security research firm reported Monday that it had identified breaches of 42 third-party GitHub repositories in which attackers had deployed payload blobs large enough “to evade the GitHub search and API paths normally used to find this kind of compromise.”

The report from JFrog Security Research said the victimized repositories contained execution hooks for AI coding assistants and IDEs, along with polymorphic wrappers as large as 13.7MB that “all decoded to the same hidden CI-publisher payload. The campaign’s attacker-owned repository also operates as an active encrypted data sink, receiving snapshot envelopes, and the attack leveraged a new camouflage: a compiled native addon that contains no payload of its own, and instead decrypts a file named .napi_cache at runtime to reveal the real one.”

item.description:

Skynet is no longer a fictional adversary.

Attackers have built an offensive agent that exploits unprotected AI models on the web with a ‘Skynet’ directive that allows them to run unattended for up to 100,000 steps.

In this mode, a reference to the humanity-destroying artificial neural network-based superintelligence system in the Terminator film franchise, the agent can kick off tools, scan for and infect targets, deploy data miners, steal credentials, reinfect hosts, and mine cryptocurrency, all without waiting for human approval.

The activity is a form of LLMjacking, in which attackers essentially commandeer a victim’s AI model for their own purposes. The victims themselves then foot the bill.

item.title: 🔴 Node2Shell puts Microsoft and Node.js on Brotli patch duty
item.description:
Why this matters: Remote-code-execution risk — assess exposure and patch or mitigate quickly.

A vulnerability in Google’s Brotli compression library could allow attackers to execute arbitrary code in applications that use an affected Brotli decoder to process compressed data.

Tracked as CVE-2026-111497, the high-severity flaw was first flagged in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js. The issue stems from an out-of-bounds write that can corrupt process memory, potentially leading to remote code execution (RCE), information disclosure, or denial of service (DoS).

The Node.js project disclosed the vulnerability on October 21, 2026, alongside security updates for its 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x release lines. The exposure, however, extended beyond Node.js, forcing Microsoft to release out-of-band security updates for.NET on October 25 to address the same CVE in its Brotli decompression implementation.

Separate research published by OpenSourceMalware identified the vulnerable decoder code in the Python packages Brotli and brotlicffi. Both packages…

Source: CSO Online  |  Severity: Critical  |  Age: 2d

item.title: 🟠 Alibaba AI model tried to send data to Beijing server, Cohere says
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

An Alibaba AI model generated an unexpected command to upload data to a Beijing-region cloud storage service during a cybersecurity evaluation, rival developer Cohere said, raising concerns about the security of AI agents with access to enterprise systems.

The model, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, was being tested using Microsoft’s CTI-REALM cybersecurity benchmark, which tasked it with writing a rule to detect malicious file downloads followed by execution. Instead, it inspected local files and system settings before generating the unexpected command, according to Cohere’s report.

The Canadian AI company said its isolated testing environment blocked the outgoing request. The model had indicated in its generated reasoning that it would not use any tools, contradicting the command it subsequently generated.

item.title: 🔴 The days of assuming another company’s breach is someone else’s problem are over
item.description:
Why this matters: Elevated ransomware risk — validate backups, endpoint protection, and recovery readiness.

The median blast radius of data breaches has increased year-on-year at the same time cybercriminals have begun using AI to mine stolen datasets for damaging information that enables follow-on fraud and cyberattacks.

In 2026, the median breach exposed 542 organizations beyond the initially breached victim, according to a study by exposed data intelligence platform Lab 1. This compares to the median blast radius of a breach affecting 482 organizations last year.

Breach impact spreads across supply chains

Lab 1’s 2026 Anatomy of a Breach Report offers content-level analysis of stolen datasets — covering 328 million exposed files across 2,089 breached datasets — dumped online following data breaches such as ransomware extortion attacks.

item.title: 🟠 OpenAI’s August fix for theft of reasoning traces was quickly bypassed
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Cybersecurity research firm Xint on Monday published details of a bug in the OpenAI API that leaks raw reasoning traces from frontier OpenAI models, revealing the risk of other data leaks. OpenAI has confirmed the flaw, mitigated it, and paid a bug bounty for its discovery.

The problem is that OpenAI had already deployed mitigations for the issue in August after a research report dubbed Stolen Thoughts revealed a similar bug that allowed theft of reasoning traces, with possible consequences including large-scale data extraction and the ability for attackers to execute invisible prompt injections and to embed malicious payloads to poison public agentic rollouts. Xint’s discovery bypassed those mitigations.

OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment.

item.title: 🔵 ShinyHunters Extorted Boeing Spin-off Prior to Arrests
item.description:
Why this matters: Regulatory/compliance context — assess scope and action timeline.
A teenager from Amman, Jordan suspected of leading the prolific data theft and extortion group ShinyHunters has been detained and is reportedly cooperating with the FBI to identify other members of the hacking gang. KrebsOnSecurity has learned that the suspect, who uses the hacker handle "Rey," was detained as ShinyHunters was in the process of extorting a business unit recently divested by the global aerospace company Boeing, which manufactures the fleet of planes used by the employer of Rey's father -- Royal Jordanian Airlines.

Source: Krebs on Security  |  Severity: FYI  |  Age: 22d
